## Chapter 1

# CHAPTER XXIX

THE ABYSS OF IGNORANCE (1902)

Spring burst into flower; Paris opened its arms. After years of effort to find one's drift, the drift found the seeker, and slowly swept him forward and back, with a steady progress oceanwards. Adams, knowing nothing of Faraday, began to mimic Faraday's trick of seeing lines of force all about him, where he had always seen lines of will. Once conceived, the image became simple, and the lines of force presented themselves as lines of attraction. By this path, the mind stepped into the mechanical theory of the universe, and entered a distinct new phase of education.

This was the work of the dynamo and the Virgin of Chartres. Like his masters, since thought began, he was handicapped by the eternal mystery of Force—the sink of all science. For thousands of years Force had been felt as occult attraction—love of God and lust for power in a future life. After 1500 the attraction declined, and philosophers fell back on some *vis a tergo*—instinct of danger from behind, like Darwin's survival of the fittest; and Pascal saw the master-motor in *ennui*: "all the troubles of man come from his not knowing how to sit still." Mere restlessness forces action.

*Ennui*, like Natural Selection, accounted for change but failed to account for direction of change. For that, an attractive force was essential; a force from outside; a shaping influence. Pascal called it God. Adams went straight to the Virgin at Chartres, and asked her to show him God, face to face, as she did for St. Bernard.

She replied, kindly as ever: "My dear outcast, what is it you seek? This is the Church of Christ! He and I are one. We are Love! We have little or nothing to do with God's other energies which are infinite, and concern us the less because our interest is only in man, and the infinite is not knowable to man. Yet if you are troubled by your ignorance, you see how I am surrounded by the masters of the schools! Ask them!"

Thomas Aquinas, unlike modern physicists, answered at once and plainly: "Christ and the Mother are one Force—Love—simple, single, and sufficient for all human wants; but Love is a human interest which acts on man so partially that you and I, as philosophers, need expect no share in it. Therefore we turn to the Schools, who deal with Multiplicity and call it God. After the Virgin has redeemed by her personal Force as Love all that is redeemable in man, the Schools embrace the rest, and give it Form, Unity, and Motive."

Rid of man and his mind, the universe of Thomas Aquinas seemed rather more scientific than that of Haeckel or Ernst Mach. Modern science offered not a vestige of proof, or a theory of connection between its forces, or any scheme of reconciliation between thought and mechanics; while St. Thomas at least linked together the joints of his machine. The thirteenth century supposed mind to be a mode of force directly derived from the intelligent prime motor, and the cause of all form and sequence. Without thought in the unit, there could be no unity; without unity no orderly sequence. Mind and Unity flourished or perished together.

This education startled even a man who had dabbled in fifty educations. If he were obliged to insist on a Universe, he seemed driven to the Church. Modern science guaranteed no unity. Yet the only honest alternative to affirming unity was to deny it; and the denial would require a new education. At sixty-five, a new education promised hardly more than the old. The pursuit of ignorance in silence had led the weary pilgrim into such mountains of ignorance that he could no longer see any path whatever, and could not even understand a signpost.

He had taken science's word that the new unit was as good as found—not an intelligence, probably not even a consciousness, but it would serve. On reviewing the ground, he was led to think that the final synthesis was the kinetic theory of gases: any portion of space occupied by molecules flying in right lines at velocities up to a mile in a second, colliding seventeen million times in a second. Unless one mistook the meaning of motion, the scientific synthesis commonly called Unity was the scientific analysis commonly called Multiplicity. The two things were the same, all forms being shifting phases of motion.

The new psychology offered no rescue. It had split personality into complex groups, like telephonic centres that might be called up at will. The compound soul took at once the form of a bicycle-rider, mechanically balancing himself by inhibiting all his inferior personalities, sure to fall into the sub-conscious chaos below if one of them got on top. His normal thought was dispersion, sleep, dream, inconsequence; the simultaneous action of different thought-centres without central control. He was an acrobat with a dwarf on his back, crossing a chasm on a slack-rope, and commonly breaking his neck.

By this path of newest science, one saw no unity ahead—nothing but a dissolving mind. Any schoolboy could see that man as a force must be measured by motion, from a fixed point. Psychology suggested a unit—the point of history when man held the highest idea of himself as a unit in a unified universe. Adams thought he might use the century 1150–1250, expressed in Amiens Cathedral and the Works of Thomas Aquinas, as the unit from which to measure motion down to his own time. He began a volume which he mentally knew as "Mont-Saint-Michel and Chartres: a Study of Thirteenth-Century Unity." From that point he proposed to fix a position which he could label: "The Education of Henry Adams: a Study of Twentieth-Century Multiplicity." Thereupon, he sailed for home.

## Chapter 2

# CHAPTER XXX

VIS INERTIAE (1903)

Washington was always amusing, but in 1900 its chief interest lay in its distance from New York. The movement of New York had become planetary—beyond control—while the task of Washington was to control it. The success of Washington in the past century promised ill for its success in the next.

Hay had reached the summit of his career, and saw himself on the edge of wreck. Committed to keeping China "open," he saw China about to be shut. Almost alone in the world, he represented the "open door," and could not escape being crushed by it. Down to that moment, the Kaiser had counted as the ally of the Czar in all matters relating to the East; this supposed alliance gave Hay no little anxiety. Suddenly Holleben, who seemed to have had no thought but to obey with agonized anxiety the least hint of the Kaiser's will, received a telegram ordering him to pretext illness and come home, which he obeyed within four-and-twenty hours. Breaking down all precedent, the Kaiser sent Speck von Sternburg in his place.

Adams had seen Hay, in 1898, bring England into his combine; he had seen the steady movement to bring France back into an Atlantic system; and now he saw the dramatic swing of Germany towards the west—the movement of all others nearest mathematical certainty. That Germany could be so quickly detached and brought into an Atlantic system seemed a paradox more paradoxical than any his education had yet offered. If Germany could be held there, a century of friction would be saved. The Kaiser, by one personal act of energy, freed Hay's hands so completely that he saw his problems simplified to Russia alone.

Russia was a problem ten times as difficult. The history of Europe for two hundred years had accomplished little but to state one or two sides of it. The drama grew every day more Byzantine; the Russian Government itself showed clear signs of dislocation. Russian diplomacy never suggested depth; Cassini could not disguise that, in setting the enormous bulk of Russian inertia to roll over China, he regretted infinitely that he should have to roll it over Hay too. His political philosophy, like that of all Russians, seemed fixed in the single idea that Russia must fatally roll—must, by her irresistible inertia, crush whatever stood in her way.

In 1903 Hay saw Russia knocking away the last blocks that held back the launch of this huge mass into the China Sea. The vast force of inertia known as China was to be united with the bulk of Russia in a single mass which no new force could deflect. The Siberian Railway offered checkmate. The wall of Russian inertia that barred Europe across the Baltic would bar America across the Pacific; and Hay's policy of the open door would infallibly fail.

The Atlantic would have to deal with a vast continental mass of inert motion, like a glacier, which moved by mechanical gravitation alone. Was volume or intensity the stronger? What and where was the *vis nova* that could hold its own before this prodigious ice-cap of *vis inertiae*?

The dictionary said inertia was a property of matter, by which matter tends, when at rest, to remain so, and, when in motion, to move on in a straight line. Finding his mind refused to imagine itself at rest or in a straight line, Adams decided that his mind moved about something it called a motive. So long as motives were habitual, the result might be called movement of inertia, to distinguish it from movement caused by newer or higher attraction.

But minds were unequally inert. Race classified thought. Race-inertia made the chief trouble in the Russian future; but surely sex-inertia had never been overcome at all. Of all movements of inertia, maternity and reproduction are the most typical. Whatever else stops, the woman must go on reproducing. If the laws of inertia are to be sought anywhere with certainty, it is in the feminine mind.

The task of accelerating or deflecting the movement of the American woman had interest infinitely greater than that of any race. With women Adams talked of little else. Sometimes, at dinner, he might ask his liveliest neighbor whether she could explain why the American woman was a failure. Without an instant's hesitation, she was sure to answer: "Because the American man is a failure!" She meant it.

Just before sailing in May, 1903, his sister-in-law, the Lodges, Mrs. Roosevelt, and Herbert came to dinner. They soon fell on his hobby with derision which stung him to pungent rejoinder: "The American man is a failure! You are all failures!" The men laughed a little—not much. Each probably made allowance for his own wife as an unusually superior woman.

The cleverer the woman, the less she denied the failure. She had failed even to hold the family together; the family was extinct like chivalry. She had been set free—volatilized like Clerk Maxwell's perfect gas; almost brought to the point of explosion, like steam. The American man had his hand on a lever and his eye on a curve in his road; his living depended on keeping up an average speed of forty miles an hour. He could not run his machine and a woman too; he must leave her, even though his wife, to find her own way.

The result was often tragic, but that was no new thing. Tragedy had been woman's lot since Eve. Her force had counted as inertia of rotation, and her axis of rotation had been the cradle and the family. If her force were diverted from its axis, it must find a new field, and the family must pay for it. So far as she succeeded, she must become sexless like the bees. For thousands of years women had rebelled—had buried themselves in the cloister, in self-sacrifice—but the American woman had no illusions or new resources, and nothing to rebel against, except her own maternity. From the male, she could look for no help; his instinct of power was blind.

Faust was helpless in the tragedy of woman. The Marguerite of the future could alone decide whether she were better off than the Marguerite of the past; whether she would rather be victim to a man, a church, or a machine.

Reading Karl Pearson's Grammar of Science and Poincaré's La Science et l'Hypothèse, Adams heard beneath their equations the whisper that order was a convenience and chaos the only honest assertion science could make of the supersensual; even Euclidian geometry, Poincaré allowed, was not true but merely convenient. Science had abandoned unity, and the child of 1900 would be born into a multiverse rather than a universe.
